conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because the postpartum weeks can bring a lot more than most people expect.

Everything we discuss is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are just ten questions, and we’ll go at your pace. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember any numbers or categories. Ready to start?

First, over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video, but it fades fast. Most of the day I’m just too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often… maybe once or twice I’ll catch myself giving a little laugh if my husband makes a joke, but it feels forced and it’s gone in a second. Mostly I feel too heavy inside to find anything truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the moment comes, it just feels flat. I’ll plan it, I’ll go, but the whole time I’m thinking, “Why don’t I feel happy?” It’s like the enjoyment part fizzles out before it even starts.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing or didn’t burp him long enough. When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying every little choice—maybe I put him down five minutes too early, maybe I’m just not cut out for this. My head knows it’s not all my fault, but the guilt still crashes over me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s breathing too fast—or not enough. I check the monitor a dozen times a night even when she’s quiet. Nothing specific happened; it’s just this constant knot that something awful is about to go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it hit me out of nowhere—like my chest tightens and I can’t catch my breath. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes and suddenly feel as if the walls are closing in. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I’m terrified and I don’t even know why.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday I almost cried because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded with one hand while she was screaming. I keep thinking, “Other moms handle this—why can’t I?” I get through it, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been almost every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she gaining enough weight, am I already failing her? I watch the clock slide past 2, then 3 a.m., and even when I doze off I jerk awake at every little sound she makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling that doesn’t really lift. I’ll look at her sweet face and feel like I *should* be glowing, but instead there’s just this ache in my chest that won’t go away.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times just since last weekend. Once was after a phone call when my mom asked how I was doing—her voice sounded so normal, and I just lost it. Another time the baby wouldn’t latch, and I sat there in the nursery with tears dripping on her blanket, feeling like I’m failing at the one thing she needs most.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed and sad, but I haven’t had thoughts like that. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-most days begin with a gray, sad mood that doesn't lift, and activities you hoped would bring joy fall flat. You're exhausted yet unable to sleep, caught in cycles of worry about your baby's safety, and often fighting sudden surges of panic. Simple tasks feel unmanageable, you blame yourself for every hiccup in infant care, and tears come often despite your deep wish to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only once or twice, feeling forced and fleeting, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes inability to experience anticipated enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intense self-blame occurring "all the time" and attributing routine infant behaviors to personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, no-trigger worries with physical anxiety symptoms and compulsive checking, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes multiple times this week with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and fear, matching "Yes, sometimes" intensity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm and inability to cope with routine tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by unhappiness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily persistent sadness ('pretty much every day') with physical heaviness and emotional pain, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes in one week, tied to feeling overwhelmed and inadequate, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score ≥14 signals probable major depressive illness; your total of 25 far exceeds this threshold. Responses map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and diminished interest most of the day (nearly every day), feelings of worthlessness/guilt, sleep disturbance, fatigue, and impaired concentration/decision-making. Additional symptoms of panic, catastrophic worries about infant well-being, and compulsive checking suggest comorbid postpartum <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health team</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments-individual <med>CBT</med>, short-term <med>IPT</med>, or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>
3. Reinforce supports: partner/family assistance with night feeds, household tasks, and scheduled rest periods
4. Encourage gentle daily structure: 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced meals, hydration, and limit monitor-checking to evidence-based intervals
5. Provide crisis resources: 24-hr Postpartum Support International helpline 1-800-944-4773 Text 'HELP' to 800-944-4773 (English/Español)
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress and adjust plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: _____________

Presenting Symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, sadness (“heavy, gray feeling” daily)  
- Marked anhedonia (laughter feels forced; anticipatory enjoyment “fizzles”)  
- Daily crying spells, often triggered by minor stressors  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re infant care (“all the time”)  
- Unwarranted anxiety about infant safety; nightly monitor checking  
- Episodic panic symptoms (chest tightness, breathlessness)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning” in routine tasks  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern & Severity  
Symptoms present most days for ≥ 2 weeks; cause subjective distress and functional difficulty with infant care.

Screening Impression  
High clinical significance for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; meets threshold for immediate follow-up assessment (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and possible referral to perinatal mental-health specialty or therapy services. Safety: negative for suicidal ideation; no current acute risk flags.
